passage:
'You haven't eaten,' Imran said, setting the plate beside her laptop.
'Twelve children in Nashik are in hospital, Imran. The biscuits from our line.' Usha's voice was flat. 'The news says they're recovering. Recovering.'
'Your factory?'
'My batches. Remember the months we skipped the full contamination test to hit dispatch? I signed off on some of them.'
Imran sat down slowly. 'What happens now?'
'Audit on Monday. My manager called. He said, "Make sure the logs are complete." You know what that means.'
'Fill in tests that never happened.'
Usha covered her face. 'If I do it, maybe no one finds out. If I don't, I'm finished. And either way, those children...'
'Usha. Look at me. Which one can you live with?'
She didn't answer. The laptop screen glowed with the empty log.

qa.q: How many children are in hospital?
qa.a: Twelve children in Nashik are in hospital.

qa.q: What is Usha feeling as she covers her face?
qa.a: She feels deep shame and fear, caught between covering up to save her job and the weight of the harm to the children.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Usha at this stage?
qa.a: She could refuse to fill in false logs and tell the auditors the truth about the skipped tests, since covering up would only add to the harm.

qa.q: What is Imran experiencing as he hears the story?
qa.a: Imran is shocked and worried for Usha, but stays steady to help her face the choice rather than make it for her.

grounding: It shows the cost of skipped tests becoming real when children fall ill and an audit looms, with shame and pressure pulling toward a cover-up.

passage:
I still remember the sound: a stack of cartons coming down, and Aditi's shout from aisle nine.
For months we had cut the second safety check on the high racks to make the evening dispatch. I was shift supervisor. I told myself the racks were fine; they always had been.
Aditi's wrist was broken. That night, standing in the car park as the ambulance lights faded, my first thought wasn't about her. It was: the inspection log. It's blank for three weeks.
I went back inside and opened the file. I actually picked up the pen.
That's the part I'm most ashamed of. Not even the shortcut. The pen.
I put it down and called the site manager instead. The next morning Aditi texted from the hospital: 'Zainab, don't blame yourself.' I did anyway.

qa.q: Where was Aditi when the cartons fell?
qa.a: Aditi was in aisle nine.

qa.q: Why is Zainab most ashamed of 'the pen'?
qa.a: Because in that moment Zainab's first instinct was to fill in the blank inspection log and hide the cause, not to think of Aditi.

qa.q: What choice at that moment shows the turning point still open?
qa.a: Putting the pen down and calling the site manager meant owning the skipped checks instead of adding a cover-up to the harm.

qa.q: How does Aditi seem to respond to Zainab afterwards?
qa.a: Aditi's text suggests she doesn't want Zainab carrying all the blame, and wants to ease that guilt even while recovering.

grounding: It shows a worker's injury making the cost of skipped checks real, and the sudden shame and urge to cover up that follow.

passage:
Wednesday, 11 p.m.
Mr Rao came to the branch today. Seventy-one years old, holding a folder. The "safe investment" plan we sold him with his home loan top-up has lost most of his savings. He asked, very politely, why nobody told him it could fall. I sold him that plan. I remember rushing through the risk page because the month-end target was due.
I couldn't look at him. I went to the washroom and cried.
Then the regional office emailed: an audit of all such sales, starting next week. Siddharth came to my desk and said quietly, "We should update the customer files. Add signed risk forms. Everyone's doing it tonight."
Part of me wanted to. It would be so easy to make it look as if we'd explained everything.
I'm sitting here with the files open, so ashamed I can't breathe properly.
Uma

qa.q: How old is Mr Rao?
qa.a: Seventy-one years old.

qa.q: What is Uma feeling with the files open?
qa.a: Uma feels deep shame and panic, tempted to cover up rather than admit what was done.

qa.q: What should Uma do instead of adding signed forms?
qa.a: Refuse to alter the files, tell the auditors or compliance the truth, and support Mr Rao in seeking redress.

qa.q: What was the visit like for Mr Rao?
qa.a: Mr Rao felt confused and hurt, politely asking why no one warned him before he lost his savings.

grounding: An elderly customer's lost savings and a looming audit make earlier choices visible, and a young employee feels shame and the pull to cover up.

Eshaan: so what do we do

qa.q: How many customers were overcharged?
qa.a: 3,000 customers overcharged for 6 months.

qa.q: What do Kunal and Eshaan feel reading the complaints?
qa.a: Both feel sick with shame and fear, seeing the real harm and the pressure to cover it up.

qa.q: Why is bringing the January ticket the right choice?
qa.a: It tells the truth about when the bug was known, instead of adding a new lie to protect the team.

qa.q: What was it like for the woman who skipped her son's school fees?

passage:
In the seed shop at Jalna, the untested hybrid packets had gone out with the old "certified" stickers. Everyone at the company knew; the lab reports were "coming soon". Siddharth had sold forty packets himself to meet the season target.
Now Bhau Patil stood at the counter with a bag of shrivelled cotton bolls and a face Siddharth would never forget. "Two acres," he said. "My daughter's college fees were in these two acres."
Siddharth's face burned. He wanted to sink through the floor.
That evening his colleague Sarika called. "The area manager says we should tell them the farmers planted too late. Everyone's saying it. There's an inspection next week."
Siddharth looked at the sales register on the table, his own handwriting on every line. He could see exactly how it would go: one small lie, then another.
He didn't sleep. At four in the morning he was still holding the register, ashamed, and not yet sure what he would do.

qa.q: How many packets did Siddharth sell himself?
qa.a: Forty packets.

qa.q: What did Siddharth feel when Bhau Patil showed the cotton bolls?
qa.a: He felt burning shame, wanting to sink through the floor at the real harm his sales had caused.

qa.q: What should Siddharth do before the inspection?
qa.a: Refuse the 'planted too late' story, tell the inspectors the truth about the stickers, and help the farmers seek compensation.

qa.q: What does the crop failure mean for Bhau Patil?
qa.a: Bhau Patil faces a painful loss, his daughter's college fees gone along with two acres of cotton.

grounding: A farmer's failed crop makes a company's shortcut visible, and a young salesman feels shame while colleagues push a cover-up.

passage: Tariq had worked in quality at the sandwich factory outside Manchester for two years, long enough to know the allergen checks had become a quick glance. On Tuesday the call came: a boy had been taken to hospital after eating one of their egg sandwiches. It had contained sesame, not listed on the label. The supermarket had already pulled the whole batch from its shelves by noon. Tariq sat in the break room with the checklists in front of him, every box ticked in his own handwriting. His face burned. Clara, the site manager, came in and shut the door. "We'll say the label printer had a fault," she said. "No need to go into the checks." Tariq opened his mouth, then closed it. He thought of the boy, and then of his own signature. He nodded, and hated himself a little for it.

qa.q: By when had the supermarket pulled the batch from its shelves?
qa.a: The supermarket had already pulled the whole batch from its shelves by noon.

qa.q: What does Tariq's burning face suggest he is feeling?
qa.a: It suggests Tariq feels deep shame, seeing his own handwriting on checks that were never really done after a boy was hurt.

qa.q: What turning point is still open to Tariq after he nods?
qa.a: Tariq could go back to Clara or to the company's safety and compliance team the same day and tell the truth about the checks, so the real cause is fixed.

qa.q: How might the boy's family be affected if the printer story is accepted?
qa.a: The family would never learn the real cause, and other families could face the same risk if the checks stay broken.

grounding: Shows a customer being hurt so the cost of earlier shortcuts becomes visible, with sudden shame and pressure to cover up rather than admit it.
